synopsis: A cold front remains stalled offshore today with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.
hydrology: The Skokomish River fell below flood stage overnight. The river will remain elevated into Friday then rise back above flood stage later Friday into the weekend with another round of heavy rain over the Olympics.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A cold front remains stalled offshore today with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Saturday)
paragraphs: Much like yesterday, a front remains stalled offshore with a very mild air mass in place across the region. Clouds will stream across the area throughout the day ahead with periods of light rainfall skirting the coast and Olympic Peninsula as the interior remains mostly dry. Models remain largely unchanged with the overall pattern heading into the conclusion of the week. A vertically stacked system moving into the offshore waters tonight and early Friday will push an occluded front onshore during the day on Friday with another shot of rain and breezy to windy conditions...especially coast and near east/west gaps in terrain. High tides and lower pressure may lead to minor coastal flooding Friday morning. The main area is the shoreline and beaches around the Salish Sea during the time of high tide. While precip with this system doesn't look particularly heavy, it should be sufficient to push the Skokomish River back above flood stage.

sections.title: Long term (Saturday night through Wednesday)
paragraphs: A stronger system remains on track to arrive later Saturday into Saturday night. More widespread windy conditions are expected with this system...strongest along the coast where NBM probabilities of 50 mph gusts are 50-70 percent. QPF is also heavier with storm total rainfall estimates between between Saturday midday and Sunday afternoon of 1.5 to 2 inches along the coast and upwards of 3 to 4 inches in the Olympics.

Showery conditions continue Sunday night into Monday before tapering off. Forecast confidence begins to decrease Tuesday and beyond as both deterministic and ensembles start to diverge with some solutions now suggesting that a system around the middle of next week will cut off and head south of the area. One portion of the forecast that retains at least some confidence is a downward trend in temperatures to nearer seasonal norms next week.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A stalled frontal boundary will remain offshore today as showers continue west of the Olympics for terminals such as KHQM and KUIL. As a result, IFR conditions will be met throughout the remainder of the morning with MVFR cigs possible for KCLM as well. Mid-high level cloud coverage will keep mostly VFR in place for inland terminals but KOLM and KPWT may have to contend with fog and low clouds throughout the remainder of the morning until conditions improve around 18-20z. VFR area wide including the coastal areas towards the afternoon but steadier widespread rain will return late overnight into Friday morning with a return of low ceilings.

KSEA...VFR likely to persist through the upcoming TAF period as high clouds stream overhead. Low chance (5%) of vicinity fog in the morning near the Duwamish River/east of the terminal this morning. Winds mainly out of the SE 5 kt or less.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A frontal boundary remains stalled offshore today as winds begin to pick up this afternoon across marine waters. A pair of strong low pressure systems will later move across the coastal waters later tonight into Friday, with the second moving through Saturday night into Sunday. As a result, the inherited Gale Watch across the coastal waters have been upgraded to a warning and a new SCA has been issued for the East Strait, starting later this morning and lasting into early Friday morning. Additional SCAs may be needed elsewhere. Seas will remain around 12 to 15 ft today before increasing above 20 ft Friday night with a 25-35% chance of seas above 25 ft through Saturday morning. An active pattern may remain into early next week as the parade of storms continue.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: The Skokomish River fell below flood stage overnight. The river will remain elevated into Friday then rise back above flood stage later Friday into the weekend with another round of heavy rain over the Olympics.
River flooding is not expected on the other rivers in the area in the next 7 days at this time. Felton/27

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: High pressure will result in dry conditions for the most locations through Thursday. An exception is the north Oregon and south Washington coast, where some light showers may clip those areas. The next storm system arrives Thursday night into Friday, returning widespread rain and gusty winds along the coast. Expect lingering showers on Saturday before the next system arrives on Sunday. A cooler and wet pattern continues into early next week. Make sure to clear storm drains and gutters of leaves and debris. If you are along the coast, beware of high surf at the end of the week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: High pressure will result in dry conditions for the most locations through Thursday. An exception is the north Oregon and south Washington coast, where some light showers may clip those areas. The next storm system arrives Thursday night into Friday, returning widespread rain and gusty winds along the coast. Expect lingering showers on Saturday before the next system arrives on Sunday. A cooler and wet pattern continues into early next week. Make sure to clear storm drains and gutters of leaves and debris. If you are along the coast, beware of high surf at the end of the week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Tuesday...Radar imagery and surface observations as of early Wednesday afternoon depicts mostly dry conditions across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington while a continuous band of light rain associated with an atmospheric river moves into the Olympic Peninsula and western British Columbia. The backside of an upper-level ridge centered over the Rockies is keeping the bulk of the precipitation north of our area and keeping us dry today and Thursday. An exception could be the Pacific County and Clatsop County coast, where there remains a 20-40% chance for light showers clipping these area. High temperatures across interior valleys are on track to the reach the mid to upper 60s this afternoon, which is several degrees above normal and could potentially break some records. Thursday will be slightly cooler as ridging gradually breaks down over our area, but highs remain forecast to peak in the low 60s across interior valleys.

Late Thursday night into Friday, the next upper-level trough will approach  the Pacific Northwest, pushing the first of a series of surface fronts through the region. This front on Friday will bring a return of widespread rain and cooler temperatures by Friday morning, with high confidence (80% chance) that the majority of places will receive at least 0.25" of rain by early Saturday morning. Chances for 24 hour rain totals exceeding 1 inch from early Friday morning to early Saturday morning are around 15-25% along the I-5 corridor, and 30-60% along the coast, with the highest chances from Tillamook southward. This system will also bring breezy winds from the south along the coast with gusts to around 30-40 mph. Chances for wind gusts exceeding 55 mph along the coast have fallen to 10-20%, so widespread power outages or downed trees along the coast appear unlikely. However, it would still be good to secure any loose outdoor items. Winds are also trending weaker along the I-5 corridor, where chances for wind gusts exceeding 40 mph have also fallen to 5-10%. Across the Cascades, snow levels around 5500 to 6500 will keep Cascade passes snow-free on Friday. This system exits the region by Friday night, with showers lingering across the area on Saturday as we receive a brief break before the next system. Snow levels briefly drop to 5000-5500 on Saturday, so there could be some light snow along Willamette Pass.

The next storm system arrives Saturday night into Sunday, bringing another  round of widespread rain and gusty coastal winds. There is still uncertainty with specific rain amounts from this system, but for now, chances for 24 hour rain totals exceeding 1 inch from Saturday evening to Sunday evening are around 40-60% along the coast and 5-10% along the I-5 corridor. Snow levels rise back above 5500 feet, keeping the passes snow- free again. Looking at early next week, ensemble guidance continues to favor a general troughing pattern across the West Coast. While the specific timing, placement, and strength of the troughing remains uncertain, this would maintain cool and unsettled pattern for our area with additional chances for precipitation.

With several rounds of rain through next week, soils will become increasingly  saturated through the weekend, potentially increasing runoff into area rivers and streams. At this time, the probability of widespread river flooding remains below 5%, though isolated flooding cannot being ruled out. In addition, any heavy rainfall could lead to ponding over roads as well as urban and small stream flooding of low-lying and poor drainage areas. While it is too early to determine specific hourly rainfall rates to assess the risk of urban flooding, residents can prepare by clearing gutters and storm drains of leaves and other debris.       -10

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Friday...A stalled frontal boundary just off the coast will remain in place through late Thursday. Southwest flow aloft will continue with mostly dry conditions across the area with the only exception along the northern OR and southwest WA coast where light rain is possible through the overnight. Thinning cloud cover across the interior lowlands has allowed for some fog to develop, impacting the typical foggy spots in the central and southern Willamette Valley and the western metro around KHIO. Some fluctuations in flight level are possible but will generally see sub-VFR conditions through 16-18z Thursday morning. Along the coast, expecting MVFR CIGs through the same time frame.
Winds overnight are expected to be light. Winds along the coast will increase tomorrow afternoon as another front approaches. Southerly winds 10-15 kt with gusts up to 25-30 kt expected.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Broken high clouds continue to stream overhead with VFR conditions expected through the TAF period. There is a low 20-30% chance for MVFR CIGs to develop late tonight around KPDX. Easterly winds around KTTD should inhibit any low cloud cover. Light easterly winds around 5 kt, except in the eastern metro around KTTD where easterly winds of 8-12 kt with gusts around 20 kt are expected to persist. -19

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A stalled frontal boundary offshore will continue to weaken through this evening into Thursday morning. Southerly winds are expected to gradually ease across the waters with gusts dropping below 30 kt by this evening. Seas of around 12 to 16 ft with a period of around 12-14 seconds are also expected to linger through Thursday morning, maintain marginal hazardous seas across the coastal waters. By Thursday afternoon, southerlies again ramp up ahead of the next low pressure system that will approach the area later Thursday into Friday. A strong Gale Force front is expected to peak early Friday morning, with south to southeasterly winds gusting over 33 kt potentially over a 24 hour period. There is also a 40-50% chance for Storm Force wind gusts to occur across the outer coastal waters during the peak timing, but probabilities remain too low to upgrade to a Storm Watch. Therefore, will maintain and extend the Gale Watch that is in effect for all coastal marine zones from Thu evening through Fri afternoon.

Seas are expected to become very steep and hazardous by Friday as a fresh south-southwesterly swell likely develops, building seas to around 14 to 18 ft with a dominant period of around 10-11 seconds. This will be followed by a strong, long-period westerly swell that is expected to build seas above 20 ft Friday afternoon, with a 40-70% chance of seas greater than 25 ft. There is also a 10-30% chance for significant wave heights reaching 30 ft in the outer waters, with highest chances to the south. Another strong front is expected to move across the waters later Saturday into Sunday with high chances for another round of strong southerly Gales, while seas remain elevated through the weekend.      /DH

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 12 to 16 ft at 14 seconds continues through Thursday. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 18 to 24 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast later Friday into Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.
